scenario: AITA for not giving my wife what she wants to eat? | I will try to keep this as concise as possible. My wife and I have been together for going on 27 years. We met at a pretty low point in both of our lives, coming from broken homes and an unhealthy dependency on food. We both probably weighed around 300lbs, and though our weight has fluctuated over the years we both currently sit at around 350lbs and 450lbs respectively, with her being the latter. I cook all the food that we eat as my wife is unable to be on her feet long enough to make meals. I am completely okay with this, as I’ve really been able to hone in on my cooking skills over the years and can essentially throw down in the kitchen. When my oldest daughter told us she was pregnant a few months back, it really made me reevaluate our lifestyle choices. I wanna be able to run around with my grandkids, but I can’t do that in my current situation. Over the course of several months I’ve been looking into healthier alternatives of our favorite foods and trying to exercise more, slowly implementing both into our lives and my wife was initially on board. More recently she’s stopped wanting to workout with me which I respected, but I’ve continued to cook healthier meals and she no longer wants to eat them. I’ve stopped buying junk and with a suspended license she can’t drive to get fast food, so I assumed she would just eat what I made like she always has. She feels like I’m forcing a lifestyle into her that she never agreed to, but I’m not pushing her to eat what I’ve made or workout. I suggested she could learn to cook what she wants and I would even help her, but I won’t continue to cook foods I no longer want to eat. Does this make me TA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is "AITA" (Ask if it's a good idea to do something) or "TA" (Too much). Let me break it down step by step. First, the person has been married for 27 years, which is a long time. Both came from tough backgrounds with issues around food and weight. They're both still heavy, but he's trying to make healthier changes. He cooks all the meals because his wife can't stand for long. He's really good at cooking, so that's a plus. He started reevaluating their lifestyle when his daughter got pregnant. He wants to be active with his grandkids, which is a common and understandable motivation. He's been looking into healthier alternatives and exercising more. Initially, his wife was on board, but lately she's pulled back. She doesn't want to work out with him anymore and doesn't want to eat the healthier meals he's preparing. He stopped buying junk food, and since she can't drive, she can't get fast food. He assumed she'd eat what he makes, but she feels he's forcing a lifestyle change on her. He offered to help her learn to cook what she wants, but he won't continue making the unhealthy foods he doesn't want to eat anymore. So, is he in the wrong here? I think about the dynamics of a long-term relationship. Both partners have their own needs and boundaries. He's making changes for his health and future, which is positive, but his wife is resisting. He's not forcing her to eat the food; he's just not making the old stuff. He's also not making her exercise. He's trying to support her by offering to teach her to cook, which shows he's considering her needs. On the other hand, she feels forced into a lifestyle change she didn't agree to. She might feel like her autonomy is being taken away, especially since she can't drive and relies on him for meals. It's possible she feels pressured even if he's not explicitly forcing her. So, is he overstepping? He's trying to improve their health, which is good, but maybe he's not considering her feelings enough. He's making changes unilaterally, which can cause friction. It's a balance between taking care of himself and respecting his wife's preferences. I think he's not entirely in the wrong because he's making positive changes for himself and offering support. However, he might need to communicate more about his intentions and be more flexible to accommodate her feelings. It's a tough spot because both partners have valid concerns.
